decks.title: Biological Classification — Part 1: Five kingdoms, Monera and Protista
goals: Explain why the two-kingdom system was replaced by the five-kingdom system
Compare the five kingdoms on cell type, cell wall, body organisation and nutrition
Describe the groups and importance of Monera
Describe the main groups of Protista

slides.heading: Biological Classification
slides.body_md: Part 1 — from two kingdoms to five, then the simplest cells: bacteria and the protists.

visual.alt: Flow of the five kingdoms from Monera and Protista to Fungi, Plantae and Animalia

slides.narration: Early biologists sorted all life into just plants and animals. As microscopes improved, that simple scheme failed. Today we use five kingdoms, and this part meets the first two: the bacteria and the protists.

slides.heading: Why two kingdoms were not enough
slides.body_md: Linnaeus placed every organism in **Plantae** or **Animalia**. This scheme did not distinguish between the **eukaryotes and prokaryotes**, **unicellular and multicellular** organisms, or **photosynthetic and non-photosynthetic** organisms.

rows: Placed with plants although they do not photosynthesise and have different walls
Photosynthesises like a plant but moves like an animal

visual.alt: Table of organisms that did not fit the two-kingdom system

slides.narration: Bacteria and fungi were counted as plants, even though they do not make their own food. Euglena has features of both plants and animals. The old scheme could not separate simple cells from complex cells, or single cells from many cells.

slides.heading: The five-kingdom classification
slides.body_md: In **1969 R. H. Whittaker** proposed five kingdoms: **Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia**. He used **cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships**.

rows: Prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Cell wall present?
Unicellular, loose tissue or tissues and organs?
Which groups share a common ancestry?

visual.alt: Table of the five criteria used by Whittaker

slides.narration: Whittaker used five kinds of evidence: cell structure, body organisation, how an organism gets food, how it reproduces, and its evolutionary relationships. Together they separated life into five kingdoms.

slides.heading: The five kingdoms
slides.body_md: **Monera** are prokaryotes. The **Protista** are unicellular eukaryotes. **Fungi**, **Plantae** and **Animalia** are multicellular eukaryotes that differ in how they obtain food.

slides.narration: Monera lie at the base because their cells have no nuclear membrane. Protista are single celled eukaryotes. From the protists three multicellular kingdoms are drawn. Fungi absorb food, plants make food, and animals ingest food.

slides.heading: Comparing the five kingdoms
slides.body_md: Compare the kingdoms on four features.

rows: chemosynthetic and photosynthetic autotrophs; saprophytic and parasitic heterotrophs

visual.alt: Table comparing the five kingdoms on cell type, cell wall, body organisation and nutrition

slides.narration: Only Monera are prokaryotic. Cell walls differ: non-cellulosic in Monera, chitin in fungi, cellulose in plants and none in animals. Plants are autotrophs, animals and fungi are heterotrophs, and Monera and Protista include both kinds.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the table
slides.body_md: A student notes that an organism is multicellular and has a cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts. Which kingdom does the table place it in?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which kingdom has cellulose walls and photosynthesis?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: placing organisms with a key
slides.body_md: Use the key: prokaryote gives Monera; otherwise unicellular gives Protista; otherwise a chitin wall gives Fungi, a cellulose wall with photosynthesis gives Plantae, and no wall with ingestion gives Animalia. Place a mushroom, Euglena and a tiger.
bullets: **Mushroom:** eukaryotic, multicellular, chitin wall: **Fungi**.
**Euglena:** eukaryotic, unicellular: **Protista**.
**Tiger:** eukaryotic, multicellular, no wall, ingests food: **Animalia**.

rows: Eukaryote, many cells, no wall, ingests food

visual.alt: Worked table placing a mushroom, Euglena and a tiger in kingdoms

slides.narration: Ask the questions in order. A mushroom is a multicellular eukaryote with a chitin wall, so it is a fungus. Euglena is a single celled eukaryote, so it is a protist. A tiger has no cell wall and takes in food, so it is an animal.

slides.body_md: **Bacteria** are the sole members of Monera. They are the most abundant organisms and occur in every kind of habitat. They are classified by shape: **coccus**, **bacillus**, **vibrio** and **spirillum**.

slides.narration: Bacteria are microscopic and live almost everywhere, from soil and water to hot springs and the inside of other organisms. By shape they are spherical cocci, rod shaped bacilli, comma shaped vibrios and spiral spirilla.

slides.heading: Archaebacteria and eubacteria
slides.body_md: **Archaebacteria** live in harsh habitats and have a different cell-wall structure. **Eubacteria** (true bacteria) have a rigid cell wall, and a flagellum if they are motile.

rows: Live in marshy areas and in the guts of ruminant animals such as cows; produce methane (biogas) from dung
Photosynthetic autotrophs; Nostoc and Anabaena fix nitrogen in heterocysts
Oxidise inorganic substances such as ammonia and nitrites for energy
Decomposers; make curd, antibiotics; fix nitrogen in legumes; some cause disease
No cell wall; smallest living cells; can live without oxygen; pathogenic

visual.alt: Table of archaebacteria, eubacteria and mycoplasma with examples

slides.narration: Archaebacteria survive in salt lakes, hot springs and marshes, where methanogens produce gas from dung. Eubacteria include cyanobacteria that photosynthesise, chemosynthetic bacteria, and the many heterotrophs. Mycoplasma are the smallest living cells and have no cell wall.

slides.heading: Quick check: heterocysts
slides.body_md: Specialised cells called heterocysts in Nostoc and Anabaena are used for which process?
slides.narration: Quick check. These cyanobacteria add a vital nutrient to soil and water.

slides.heading: Bacteria in our lives
slides.body_md: Most bacteria are **heterotrophs**, and many are **decomposers**. Others help or harm us.

rows: Diseases of farm animals and pets

visual.alt: Table of helpful and harmful bacteria

slides.narration: Heterotrophic bacteria are the commonest. They decompose dead matter, turn milk into curd, supply antibiotics and fix nitrogen in the roots of legumes. Some cause cholera, typhoid, tetanus and citrus canker.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: growth by binary fission
slides.body_md: Bacteria multiply by **fission**. One cell has a generation time of 30 minutes. How many cells exist after 3 hours if growth is unchecked?
bullets: Generations $= \dfrac{180}{30} = 6$.
Cells $= 1 \times 2^{6} = 64$.
In real life food runs out, so growth soon slows.

visual.alt: Worked table of cell numbers: 64 cells after 6 generations

slides.narration: Divide the total time by the generation time to find how many times the population doubles. Here that is six doublings. One cell becomes sixty four cells. In nature food and space run out, so growth slows down.

slides.narration: Protists are single celled eukaryotes with a nucleus and other organelles. Many move by cilia or flagella. Amoeba uses pseudopodia, Paramecium has cilia, Euglena has a flagellum, and a diatom has a glassy silica shell.

slides.heading: Groups of protists
slides.body_md: Each group has a distinctive feature.

rows: Diatoms and golden algae; diatom walls of silica are indestructible, leaving diatomaceous earth; chief producers in the oceans
Mostly marine photosynthetic; two flagella; rapid multiplication makes red tides (Gonyaulax) that can kill fish
Freshwater; no cell wall but a protein-rich pellicle; photosynthetic in light, heterotrophic without it
Saprophytic; form a plasmodium and spore-bearing fruiting bodies

visual.alt: Table of the five groups of protists with features and examples

slides.narration: Diatoms have silica shells. Dinoflagellates can multiply so fast that the sea turns red. Euglena photosynthesises in light and feeds on other organisms in the dark. Protozoans are heterotrophic and include the parasites of sleeping sickness and malaria.

slides.heading: Quick check: Euglena
slides.body_md: Why is Euglena difficult to place in either plants or animals?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about how it gets food in light and in the dark.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Two kingdoms failed to separate prokaryotes from eukaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, and autotrophs from heterotrophs.
Whittaker (1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
Monera: bacteria; coccus, bacillus, vibrio, spirillum; archaebacteria and eubacteria; mycoplasma.
Cyanobacteria fix nitrogen in heterocysts; bacteria reproduce by fission.
Protista: chrysophytes, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds, protozoans.

visual.alt: Summary table of Monera and Protista

slides.narration: To recap: Whittaker proposed five kingdoms using several kinds of evidence. Monera are prokaryotic bacteria. Protista are single celled eukaryotes in five groups. Both kingdoms include autotrophs and heterotrophs.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the **five kingdoms**, the **year** and **Whittaker**.
For each kingdom state **cell type, wall, organisation and nutrition**.
Give **one example** for each group of Monera and Protista.
Show the **doubling sum** for bacterial growth in two steps.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Know the five kingdoms and who proposed them. Compare them on cell type, wall, body organisation and nutrition. Learn one example for each group of bacteria and protists. And write growth sums as generations first, then cells.

slides.heading: How fungi feed
slides.body_md: Fungi are **heterotrophs**. They absorb soluble organic matter from the substrate.

rows: Lichens with algae; mycorrhiza with roots of higher plants

visual.alt: Table of saprophytic, parasitic and symbiotic fungi

slides.narration: Fungi cannot make their own food. Saprophytes absorb nutrients from dead matter. Parasites feed on living hosts. Symbionts live in partnership, as in lichens, which pair a fungus with an alga, and mycorrhiza on plant roots.

slides.heading: Reproduction in fungi
slides.body_md: Fungi reproduce in **three** ways.

rows: Oospores, ascospores or basidiospores, formed after plasmogamy and karyogamy

visual.alt: Table of vegetative, asexual and sexual reproduction in fungi

slides.narration: Fungi can multiply by breaking, splitting or budding. They make asexual spores such as conidia. Sexual reproduction forms oospores, ascospores or basidiospores. Yeast is a familiar budding fungus.

slides.heading: The sexual cycle
slides.body_md: **Plasmogamy** is the fusion of cytoplasm. **Karyogamy** is the fusion of two nuclei. In Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes a **dikaryon** stage with two nuclei in each cell comes between them.

visual.alt: Flow of the fungal sexual cycle from haploid hyphae to haploid spores

slides.narration: Haploid hyphae meet and their cytoplasm fuses, which is plasmogamy. In some fungi the two nuclei then live together in a dikaryon. When they fuse, in karyogamy, a diploid zygote forms. Meiosis then makes haploid spores.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: chromosome numbers in the cycle
slides.body_md: A fungus has 8 chromosomes in each haploid nucleus. Find the number in each nucleus and in the whole cell at the dikaryon stage, in the zygote nucleus, and in the spores.
bullets: Dikaryon: two nuclei, each with 8, so **16** chromosomes per cell, but each nucleus is still haploid.
Karyogamy gives a diploid zygote nucleus with **16** chromosomes.
Meiosis restores **8** chromosomes in each spore.

visual.alt: Worked table of chromosome numbers: 8, 8 in each of two nuclei, 16 and 8

slides.narration: In the dikaryon stage the two nuclei stay separate, so each is still haploid. Fusion at karyogamy doubles the number in a single nucleus. Meiosis halves it again, so every spore is haploid.

slides.heading: Four classes of fungi
slides.body_md: Fungi are placed in four classes: Phycomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes, Deuteromycetes.

rows: Aseptate, coenocytic mycelium; zoospores or aplanospores; zygospores
Septate mycelium; conidia; ascospores in asci
Penicillium, Aspergillus, Neurospora; yeast is unicellular
Septate; no asexual spores; four basidiospores on a basidium
Imperfect fungi: only asexual stage known; conidia

visual.alt: Table of the four classes of fungi with features and examples

slides.narration: Phycomycetes have tubes without cross walls. Ascomycetes make ascospores inside sacs called asci. Basidiomycetes make four basidiospores on a basidium and include mushrooms. Deuteromycetes are called imperfect because only their asexual stage is known.

slides.heading: Lichens as pollution indicators
slides.body_md: Lichens are very sensitive to **air pollution** and do not grow in polluted areas, so they are **pollution indicators**.

rows: Polluted air, for example in a busy city centre

visual.alt: Table of lichen growth and air quality

slides.narration: Lichens cannot tolerate polluted air. Where they grow richly, the air is clean. Where they are few or absent, pollution is likely, so lichens act as living pollution indicators.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a lichen survey
slides.body_md: Lichen cover on tree trunks along a road out of a city is: City centre 2 percent, Suburb 10 percent, Village 34 percent, Forest 60 percent. How many times greater is the cover in the forest than in the city centre, and what does the trend show?
bullets: $\dfrac{60}{2} = 30$ times.
Cover rises steadily away from the city, as the air becomes cleaner.
So lichens indicate the level of **air pollution**.

visual.alt: Worked table of lichen cover rising from 2 to 60 percent away from the city

slides.narration: Divide the forest value by the city centre value to find how many times greater it is. The cover rises as we move away from the city, which shows that the air gets cleaner. This is why lichens are pollution indicators.

slides.body_md: Viruses were not in the Whittaker scheme. They are **nucleoproteins**, **inert outside** a living cell, and **replicate only inside a host**.

rows: Sap of diseased tobacco still infected plants after filtering out bacteria
Called the infectious fluid contagium vivum fluidum (a living infectious fluid)
Crystallised a virus; the crystals were largely protein

slides.narration: Ivanowsky found that sap of diseased tobacco plants stayed infectious after bacteria were filtered out. Beijerinck called it a living infectious fluid. Stanley crystallised the virus, showing that it could be inert and largely made of protein.

notes.title: Biological Classification — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The five-kingdom classification
sections.body_md:
Early classification placed every organism in one of two kingdoms, **Plantae** or **Animalia** (Linnaeus). That scheme did not distinguish between **eukaryotes and prokaryotes**, **unicellular and multicellular** organisms, or **photosynthetic (green) and non-photosynthetic (non-green)** organisms; bacteria and fungi were counted with plants, and organisms such as *Euglena* did not fit either kingdom.

In **1969** **R. H. Whittaker** proposed a **five-kingdom classification**: **Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia**. The criteria were **cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships**.

| Kingdom | Cell type | Cell wall | Body organisation | Nutrition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monera | prokaryotic | non-cellulosic (polysaccharide with amino acids) | cellular | chemosynthetic and photosynthetic autotrophs; saprophytic and parasitic heterotrophs |
| Protista | eukaryotic | present in some | cellular | photosynthetic autotrophs; heterotrophs (predators, parasites) |
| Fungi | eukaryotic | chitin and polysaccharides | multicellular, loose tissue | heterotrophic: saprophytes, parasites, symbionts |
| Plantae | eukaryotic | cellulose | tissues and organs | photosynthetic autotrophs (few heterotrophs) |
| Animalia | eukaryotic | absent | tissues, organs and organ systems | holozoic (ingest and digest food) |

Only **Monera** are prokaryotic, so only they lack a nuclear membrane. **Protista** are unicellular eukaryotes. **Fungi**, **Plantae** and **Animalia** are multicellular (Fungi with loose tissue), and differ in how they obtain food: fungi absorb it, plants make it by photosynthesis, and animals ingest it. **Plantae** have cellulose cell walls, chloroplasts and autotrophic nutrition (a few are insectivorous or parasitic, such as *Cuscuta*) and show alternation of generations. **Animalia** are heterotrophic (holozoic), lack cell walls and usually show sexual reproduction with embryonic development. (Plant and animal kingdoms are studied in detail in later chapters; the five-kingdom scheme shown here keeps viruses and viroids outside it.)

sections.heading: 2. Monera, Protista and Fungi
sections.body_md:
**Kingdom Monera.** Bacteria are the sole members of Monera. They are the most abundant micro-organisms and occur in almost every habitat. **Shapes:** spherical **coccus**, rod-shaped **bacillus**, comma-shaped **vibrio** and spiral **spirillum**. Nutrition may be **autotrophic** (photosynthetic or chemosynthetic) or **heterotrophic** (saprophytic or parasitic). Bacteria reproduce mainly by **fission**; under unfavourable conditions some form spores, and a primitive form of sexual reproduction transfers DNA from one bacterium to another.
- **Archaebacteria** have a different cell-wall structure and live in harsh habitats: **halophiles** (very salty areas), **thermoacidophiles** (hot springs) and **methanogens** (marshy areas and the guts of ruminants such as cows, where they produce methane, the basis of biogas from dung).
- **Eubacteria** (true bacteria) have a rigid cell wall and a flagellum if motile. **Cyanobacteria** (blue-green algae) are photosynthetic autotrophs, unicellular, colonial or filamentous; *Nostoc* and *Anabaena* fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called **heterocysts**. **Chemosynthetic autotrophs** oxidise inorganic substances (nitrates, nitrites, ammonia) for energy and recycle nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and sulphur. **Heterotrophic bacteria** are the most abundant and mostly decomposers; they make curd, provide antibiotics and fix nitrogen in legume roots, but some cause **cholera, typhoid, tetanus** and **citrus canker**.
- **Mycoplasma** completely lack a cell wall, are the smallest living cells known, can live without oxygen and are pathogenic in animals and plants.

**Kingdom Protista.** All single-celled eukaryotes are protists; the boundary with other kingdoms is not well defined, and they form a link between monera, plants, animals and fungi.
- **Chrysophytes:** diatoms and golden algae; diatom cell walls of **silica** are in two overlapping halves and indestructible, leaving **diatomaceous earth**; chief producers in the oceans.
- **Dinoflagellates:** mostly marine and photosynthetic, with two flagella; rapid multiplication of species such as *Gonyaulax* causes **red tides** that can kill fish.
- **Euglenoids:** mostly freshwater; no cell wall but a protein-rich **pellicle**; photosynthetic in light and heterotrophic when deprived of light.
- **Slime moulds:** saprophytic; form a **plasmodium** and fruiting bodies with resistant spores dispersed by air.
- **Protozoans:** heterotrophs (predators or parasites): **amoeboid** (*Amoeba*, pseudopodia; *Entamoeba* parasitic), **flagellated** (*Trypanosoma*, sleeping sickness), **ciliated** (*Paramecium*) and **sporozoans** (*Plasmodium*, malaria).

**Kingdom Fungi.** Fungi are **heterotrophic**: **saprophytes** (dead matter), **parasites** (living hosts) or **symbionts** (lichens and mycorrhiza). The body is made of **hyphae**, whose network is the **mycelium**; hyphae may be **coenocytic** (aseptate, many nuclei) or **septate**. Cell walls are **chitin** and polysaccharides. **Reproduction:** vegetative (fragmentation, fission, budding); asexual (conidia, sporangiospores, zoospores); sexual (oospores, ascospores, basidiospores) through **plasmogamy**, an optional **dikaryon** stage (n + n) in Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes, **karyogamy** and **meiosis**.
- **Phycomycetes:** aseptate coenocytic mycelium; zoospores or aplanospores; zygospore; *Mucor*, *Rhizopus*, *Albugo*.
- **Ascomycetes (sac fungi):** septate; conidia; ascospores in **asci**; *Penicillium*, *Aspergillus*, *Claviceps*, *Neurospora*; yeast is unicellular; morels and truffles are edible.
- **Basidiomycetes:** mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs, rusts and smuts; septate; no asexual spores; four **basidiospores** on a **basidium**; *Agaricus*, *Ustilago*, *Puccinia*.
- **Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi):** only the asexual (conidial) phase is known; *Alternaria*, *Colletotrichum*, *Trichoderma*.

sections.heading: 3. Lichens, viruses and viroids
sections.body_md:
**Lichens** are **symbiotic associations** between an **alga** (the **phycobiont**) and a **fungus** (the **mycobiont**). The alga prepares food by photosynthesis; the fungus provides shelter, absorbs water and minerals and protects the alga. Lichens are very sensitive to **air pollution** and do not grow in polluted areas, so they are used as **pollution indicators**.

**Viruses** were not included in the Whittaker scheme because they are not truly cellular. The name means venom or poisonous fluid. Milestones: **D. J. Ivanowsky (1892)** found that the sap of diseased tobacco plants could still infect healthy plants after passing through a filter that stops bacteria; **M. W. Beijerinck (1898)** showed that the infectious fluid could multiply in the host and called it *contagium vivum fluidum* (living infectious fluid); **W. M. Stanley (1935)** crystallised the virus and found the crystals largely protein. Viruses are **nucleoproteins**: a **protein coat (capsid)** made of subunits (**capsomeres**) surrounds the genetic material, which is **RNA or DNA** (never both). They are inert outside the host and **replicate only inside a living host cell**, taking over its machinery. Most plant viruses have single-stranded RNA; animal viruses may have single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA; **bacteriophages** (viruses that attack bacteria) have double-stranded DNA. Diseases: mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza and AIDS in humans; mosaic formation, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing and vein clearing, dwarfing and stunted growth in plants.

**Viroids** were discovered by **T. O. Diener (1971)** as the cause of **potato spindle tuber disease**. A viroid is **free RNA of low molecular weight** and has **no protein coat**; it is smaller than a virus. (Whether viruses are living is debated: they have genetic material and evolve, but show life only inside a host.)

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving the year of the five-kingdom scheme wrongly or crediting it to Linnaeus (Whittaker proposed it in 1969).
- Placing bacteria in the plant kingdom; Monera are prokaryotes.
- Mixing up archaebacteria (halophiles, thermoacidophiles, methanogens) and eubacteria (cyanobacteria and others).
- Saying that cyanobacteria fix nitrogen everywhere; only in heterocysts (as in Nostoc and Anabaena).
- Confusing coenocytic hyphae (no septa) with septate hyphae, or plasmogamy with karyogamy.
- Writing that the dikaryon is diploid; each nucleus is still haploid (n + n).
- Giving the wrong number of basidiospores (four per basidium) or placing yeast outside the Ascomycetes.
- Saying viruses have both DNA and RNA, or that viroids have a protein coat.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: kingdom of an organism, an example, a scientist and year, a spore type, a heterocyst, a viroid fact; assertion-reason on classification.
- 2–3-mark answers: why the two-kingdom system failed; archaebacteria with examples; features of a protist group; plasmogamy, dikaryon and karyogamy; lichens; viruses versus viroids.
- 5-mark answers: the five kingdoms compared; Monera with groups and importance; the four classes of fungi; viruses and viroids with discovery.
- Case-based items: surveys with percentages, bacterial growth, spore counts, lichen cover, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: A student notes that an organism is multicellular, has a cellulose cell wall and has chloroplasts. According to the five-kingdom scheme, which kingdom should she place it in?
questions.solution_md: Multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose walls and photosynthesis belong to Plantae; fungi have chitin walls and no chloroplasts — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A botanist in the 1900s labels a mould growing on bread, a photosynthetic Euglena and a rose all as “plants”. Which weakness of the two-kingdom system does this show?

options.text_md: It placed all animals in the plant kingdom.
It had too many kingdoms for students to remember.
It did not separate photosynthetic from non-photosynthetic organisms or unicellular from multicellular ones.
It separated prokaryotes from eukaryotes too strictly.

questions.solution_md: The two-kingdom system did not distinguish eukaryotes from prokaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, or photosynthetic from non-photosynthetic forms — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The five-kingdom classification was proposed by
questions.solution_md: R. H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom scheme in 1969 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A lab technician finds that the cell walls of an organism contain chitin. In which kingdom is it placed?
questions.solution_md: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin and polysaccharides — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A quiz question asks for the pair of kingdoms that each include both autotrophic and heterotrophic members. Which pair is correct?
questions.solution_md: Monera and Protista each contain autotrophs (photosynthetic, and in Monera chemosynthetic) and heterotrophs — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student examines a pond organism with a microscope: it has a well-formed nucleus, is a single cell, and swims using cilia. Using the five-kingdom key, which kingdom is it?
questions.solution_md: A single-celled eukaryote belongs to Protista (here a ciliate such as Paramecium) — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bacteria and fungi were wrongly grouped with plants in the two-kingdom system.

**Reason (R):** Bacteria and fungi do not photosynthesise, and their cell walls differ from those of plants.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the lack of photosynthesis and the different walls show that these organisms do not belong with plants — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Monera are placed in a kingdom of their own.

**Reason (R):** Kingdom Monera contains multicellular organisms with a true nucleus.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: bacteria differ from all other organisms in being prokaryotes. R is false: Monera are mostly unicellular and have no true nucleus — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the five-kingdom scheme, every kingdom except Monera is made up of eukaryotes.
questions.solution_md: True: Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia are eukaryotic; Monera are prokaryotic.

questions.stem_md: The kingdom whose cells have no nuclear membrane is ______.
questions.solution_md: Monera.

questions.stem_md: Match each kingdom (column I) with a feature (column II).

match_right.text_md: No cell wall; food is ingested

questions.solution_md: Fungi: chitin; Plantae: cellulose wall and chloroplasts; Animalia: no wall, food ingested; Monera: no nuclear membrane.

questions.stem_md: Using the five-kingdom table, in how many of the five kingdoms are there organisms that make their own food (autotrophs)?
questions.solution_md: Monera (photosynthetic and chemosynthetic bacteria), Protista (photosynthetic protists) and Plantae: 3 kingdoms.

questions.stem_md: A student says, “Euglena is a plant because it photosynthesises.” Explain why Euglena is difficult to place in a two-kingdom system, and where it is placed in the five-kingdom system.

answer.model_answer_md: *Euglena* photosynthesises in light like a plant but becomes **heterotrophic** in the dark and has **no cell wall**, only a protein-rich pellicle, and it moves by a flagellum like an animal, so it fits neither kingdom. In the five-kingdom system it is a **unicellular eukaryote** and is placed in **Protista**.

questions.solution_md: Features of both; Protista.

questions.stem_md: List four of the criteria that Whittaker used to define the five kingdoms.

answer.model_answer_md: Whittaker used five criteria. They were **cell structure** (prokaryotic or eukaryotic, wall present or absent), **body organisation** (cellular, loose tissue or tissues and organs), **mode of nutrition**, **reproduction** and **phylogenetic (evolutionary) relationships**; any four are enough.

questions.solution_md: Any four criteria.

questions.stem_md: Compare Plantae, Fungi and Animalia on their cell wall, mode of nutrition and body organisation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Plantae:** cellulose cell wall; autotrophic by photosynthesis; tissues and organs. **Fungi:** chitin and polysaccharide wall; heterotrophic by absorption (saprophytes, parasites, symbionts); multicellular with loose tissue (hyphae). **Animalia:** no cell wall; heterotrophic, food is ingested and digested (holozoic); tissues, organs and organ systems.

questions.solution_md: Three kingdoms on three features.

questions.stem_md: A team finds three organisms: X, a single-celled eukaryote that photosynthesises; Y, a multicellular eukaryote with chitin walls that absorbs food; Z, a single-celled prokaryote with a peptidoglycan wall. Place each in a kingdom and give one reason.

answer.model_answer_md: **X** belongs to **Protista**: it is a **unicellular eukaryote** with a nucleus, even though it photosynthesises like a plant. **Y** belongs to **Fungi**: it has **chitin walls**, a multicellular body and **absorptive heterotrophic** nutrition. **Z** belongs to **Monera**: it is a **prokaryote**, so it has no nuclear membrane and no membrane-bound organelles.

questions.solution_md: Three placements with reasons.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the five-kingdom classification replaced the two-kingdom system. Name the five kingdoms and compare them on cell type, cell wall, body organisation and mode of nutrition.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Why the change.** Linnaeus’s two kingdoms, Plantae and Animalia, did not distinguish between eukaryotes and prokaryotes, unicellular and multicellular organisms, or photosynthetic and non-photosynthetic organisms. Bacteria and fungi were counted as plants although they do not photosynthesise, and organisms like Euglena fitted neither kingdom.

**The scheme.** R. H. Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969, using cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

**Comparison.** **Monera:** prokaryotic; non-cellulosic wall; cellular; autotrophic or heterotrophic. **Protista:** eukaryotic; wall present in some; cellular; autotrophic or heterotrophic. **Fungi:** eukaryotic; chitin wall; multicellular with loose tissue; heterotrophic. **Plantae:** eukaryotic; cellulose wall; tissues and organs; autotrophic. **Animalia:** eukaryotic; no wall; tissues, organs and organ systems; heterotrophic.

In the same swab of 80 cells, 32 are cocci. What percentage of the cells are cocci?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{32}{80} \times 100 = 40$ percent.

questions.stem_md: A culture starts with 4 bacterial cells with a generation time of 20 minutes. How many cells are present after 120 minutes if growth is unchecked?
questions.solution_md: Generations $= \dfrac{120}{20} = 6$; cells $= 4 \times 2^{6} = 256$.

questions.stem_md: Name the three groups of archaebacteria and state the habitat of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Halophiles** live in extremely **salty** areas; **thermoacidophiles** live in **hot, acidic springs**; **methanogens** live in **marshy areas** and in the **guts of ruminants** such as cows, producing methane.

questions.solution_md: Three groups with habitats.

questions.stem_md: Give two features of mycoplasma that make them different from other bacteria.

answer.model_answer_md: Mycoplasma **completely lack a cell wall**, so they can change shape; they are the **smallest living cells** known and can **survive without oxygen**. They are **pathogenic** to animals and plants.

questions.solution_md: Any two features.

questions.stem_md: A farmer finds that a pond covered with Nostoc and Anabaena enriches the rice field when its water is used for irrigation. Explain the role of these organisms.

answer.model_answer_md: *Nostoc* and *Anabaena* are **cyanobacteria** that **fix atmospheric nitrogen** in their specialised cells, the **heterocysts**, so they add **nitrogen compounds** to the water and soil that crop plants can use. They are also **photosynthetic autotrophs**.

questions.solution_md: Nitrogen fixation in heterocysts.

questions.stem_md: Describe three ways in which heterotrophic bacteria help humans and two ways in which they harm them.

answer.model_answer_md: **Helpful:** bacteria **make curd** from milk; they **produce antibiotics**; they **fix nitrogen** in the roots of legumes; and as **decomposers** they recycle nutrients. **Harmful:** some cause diseases in humans such as **cholera, typhoid and tetanus**, and in plants such as **citrus canker**.

questions.solution_md: Three benefits, two harms.

questions.stem_md: Compare the photosynthetic, chemosynthetic and heterotrophic modes of nutrition in Monera, with one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Photosynthetic:** cyanobacteria make food using light, as in *Nostoc*. **Chemosynthetic:** bacteria oxidise **inorganic substances** such as ammonia and nitrites and use the energy to make food; they recycle nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and sulphur. **Heterotrophic:** bacteria such as the curd bacterium absorb food made by others, as **saprophytes or parasites**.

questions.solution_md: Three modes with examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe kingdom Monera. Include the shapes of bacteria, the two main groups with their subgroups, the modes of nutrition, reproduction, and the roles of bacteria in nature and human life.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Features.** Bacteria are the sole members of Monera. They are prokaryotes and the most abundant micro-organisms, occurring in every kind of habitat. By shape they are **coccus** (spherical), **bacillus** (rod), **vibrio** (comma) and **spirillum** (spiral).

**Groups.** **Archaebacteria** have a different cell-wall structure and live in harsh habitats: halophiles in very salty areas, thermoacidophiles in hot springs and methanogens in marshes and the guts of ruminants, producing methane. **Eubacteria** have a rigid cell wall: cyanobacteria (photosynthetic; *Nostoc* and *Anabaena* fix nitrogen in heterocysts), chemosynthetic autotrophs, and heterotrophs. Mycoplasma lack a cell wall.

**Nutrition.** Autotrophic (photosynthetic or chemosynthetic) or heterotrophic (saprophytic or parasitic).

**Reproduction.** Mainly by fission; some form spores in unfavourable conditions, and DNA may be transferred between cells.

**Roles.** Decomposers and nutrient recyclers; curd, antibiotics and nitrogen fixation in legumes; pathogens causing cholera, typhoid, tetanus and citrus canker.

questions.solution_md: Shapes; groups; nutrition; reproduction; roles.

questions.stem_md: Why is Euglena difficult to place in either the plant or the animal kingdom of the old two-kingdom system?

options.text_md: It photosynthesises in light but feeds on other organisms in the dark, and it has no cell wall.
It has a nucleus but no cytoplasm.
It has a cellulose cell wall but moves by muscles.
It is multicellular and lives only on land.

questions.solution_md: Euglena has chloroplasts and photosynthesises in light, becomes heterotrophic without light, and has a flexible pellicle, not a wall — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A factory filters sugar syrup through a fine, chemically inert earth made of fossil shells of microscopic organisms. Which protists left these shells?
questions.solution_md: Diatoms have indestructible silica walls that remain as diatomaceous earth, used for filtering — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Fishermen on a coast see the sea turn red and many fish die. The cause is the rapid multiplication of which protists?
questions.solution_md: Red tides are caused by rapid multiplication of dinoflagellates like Gonyaulax, whose toxins can kill fish — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A gardener sees a yellow, jelly-like mass creeping over decaying leaves and later forming small stalks with spores. To which group of protists does it belong?
questions.solution_md: Slime moulds are saprophytic protists that form a plasmodium moving over decaying matter and later spore-bearing fruiting bodies — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Plasmodium, which causes malaria, has an infectious spore-like stage. To which group of protozoans does it belong?
questions.solution_md: Plasmodium is a sporozoan — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A parasite that causes sleeping sickness moves with a long flagellum. In which group of protozoans is Trypanosoma placed?
questions.solution_md: Trypanosoma is a flagellated protozoan — option (a).

**Assertion (A):** The cell walls of diatoms remain in large deposits long after the organisms have died.

**Reason (R):** The cell walls of diatoms are made of silica, which is indestructible.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The kingdom Protista forms a link between the other kingdoms.

**Reason (R):** All protists are multicellular organisms with cell walls of cellulose.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: protists are unicellular eukaryotes and many have no cell wall or a different wall — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Paramecium moves with the help of cilia, whereas Amoeba moves with pseudopodia.
questions.solution_md: True: Paramecium is a ciliated protozoan and Amoeba an amoeboid protozoan.

questions.stem_md: Euglenoids have no cell wall but a flexible protein-rich layer called the ______.
questions.solution_md: Pellicle.

questions.stem_md: Match each protist (column I) with its feature (column II).
questions.solution_md: Amoeba: pseudopodia; Paramecium: cilia; Trypanosoma: flagellum; diatom: silica wall in two halves.

questions.stem_md: A plankton sample of 100 unicellular organisms has 45 diatoms, 30 dinoflagellates, 15 euglenoids and 10 others. What percentage are diatoms?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{45}{100} \times 100 = 45$ percent.

questions.stem_md: Why is the boundary of kingdom Protista said to be “not well defined”, and what does the kingdom link?

answer.model_answer_md: Protista contains very different **unicellular eukaryotes**, some photosynthetic like plants and some heterotrophic like animals, with features that overlap other kingdoms, so its **boundary is not well defined**. It forms a **connecting link** between **monera, plants, animals and fungi**.

questions.solution_md: Overlapping features; link.

questions.stem_md: Name the structure that supports Euglena in place of a cell wall and describe how it feeds in bright light and in the dark.

answer.model_answer_md: Euglena has a **pellicle**, a flexible protein-rich layer. In **bright light** it is **photosynthetic**, using its chloroplasts; in the **dark** it becomes **heterotrophic** and feeds on other small organisms.

questions.solution_md: Pellicle; two modes.

questions.stem_md: Explain how a “red tide” forms and why it harms marine life.

answer.model_answer_md: Some **dinoflagellates**, such as *Gonyaulax*, **multiply very rapidly** and their pigments turn the sea water **red**. Their **toxins** released into the water can **kill other marine animals such as fish**.

questions.solution_md: Rapid multiplication; toxins.

questions.stem_md: Name four groups of protozoans and give one example and one distinguishing feature of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Protozoans are heterotrophic protists, living as predators or parasites. **Amoeboid:** *Amoeba* moves and feeds by **pseudopodia**. **Flagellated:** *Trypanosoma* has **flagella** and causes sleeping sickness. **Ciliated:** *Paramecium* has **cilia** that create a water current carrying food into the gullet. **Sporozoans:** *Plasmodium* has an **infectious spore-like stage** and causes malaria.

questions.solution_md: Four groups with examples and features.

questions.stem_md: Describe kingdom Protista. Name its main groups and, for each, give the distinguishing features and at least one example. Mention one harmful and one beneficial effect of protists.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Features.** Protista are unicellular eukaryotes with a nucleus and other organelles. The boundary with other kingdoms is not well defined, and they link monera, plants, animals and fungi.

**Groups.** **Chrysophytes:** diatoms and golden algae; diatom walls are indestructible silica in two halves, forming diatomaceous earth; chief producers in the oceans. **Dinoflagellates:** mostly marine and photosynthetic with two flagella; *Gonyaulax* blooms cause red tides. **Euglenoids:** mostly freshwater; protein-rich pellicle; photosynthetic in light, heterotrophic in the dark; *Euglena*. **Slime moulds:** saprophytic; plasmodium; spore-bearing fruiting bodies. **Protozoans:** heterotrophic predators or parasites: *Amoeba* (pseudopodia), *Trypanosoma* (flagella), *Paramecium* (cilia) and *Plasmodium* (spore-like stage).

**Effects.** Beneficial: diatoms are chief ocean producers and diatomaceous earth is used for filtering. Harmful: red tides kill fish, and parasitic protozoans cause sleeping sickness and malaria.

questions.solution_md: Features; groups; effects.

marking_scheme.step: One harmful and one beneficial effect

questions.solution_md: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin and polysaccharides — option (a).

questions.solution_md: After plasmogamy, the cell with two genetically different haploid nuclei is a dikaryon (n + n); karyogamy follows later — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Describe the discovery, structure and nature of viruses. Include the work of Ivanowsky, Beijerinck and Stanley, the genetic material of plant, animal and bacterial viruses, and some diseases caused.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Discovery.** D. J. Ivanowsky (1892) found that the sap of diseased tobacco plants still infected healthy plants after filtering out bacteria. M. W. Beijerinck (1898) called the fluid contagium vivum fluidum. W. M. Stanley (1935) crystallised the virus and found the crystals largely protein.

**Structure.** A virus is a nucleoprotein: genetic material, RNA or DNA but not both, enclosed in a protein coat, the capsid, made of capsomeres. Most plant viruses have single-stranded RNA; animal viruses have single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA; bacteriophages have double-stranded DNA.

**Nature.** Outside a host a virus is inert and can be crystallised; inside a living host cell it uses the host’s machinery to replicate. For this reason viruses are not placed in the five kingdoms.

**Diseases.** Mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza and AIDS in humans; mosaic, leaf curling, yellowing and stunting in plants.

questions.stem_md: A magazine writes: “Viruses should be added as a sixth kingdom because they reproduce and evolve, so they are clearly alive.” Evaluate this claim using what you know about the nature of viruses, lichens and viroids, and state whether the five-kingdom scheme should be changed.

answer.model_answer_md:
**What the claim gets right.** Viruses carry genetic material (DNA or RNA), they replicate, and they evolve; so they do have some features of life.

**What it misses.** Viruses are **not cellular**: a protein coat surrounds nucleic acid, and there is no cytoplasm or ribosomes. Outside a host a virus is **inert** and can even be **crystallised** (Stanley, 1935). It **replicates only inside a living host cell**, using the host’s machinery. Whittaker’s kingdoms were built on **cell structure, nutrition and body organisation**, and viruses fit none of these criteria. Viroids, which are only free RNA, show the same problem even more clearly.

**Other special cases.** Lichens are partnerships of two organisms, an alga and a fungus, and also sit uneasily in a single kingdom, yet they are not given a kingdom.

**Judgement.** The claim is only partly sound. Viruses are special cases that are **kept outside** the five kingdoms rather than made a sixth, because they lack a cellular structure and cannot live independently. Whether they are “alive” remains debated.

questions.solution_md: What is right; what is missed; special cases; judgement.

marking_scheme.step: Criteria of the kingdoms; viroids and lichens
